The core architecture is now mostly built. The remaining gap is proving it under sustained real-world use and integrating the latest large hardening tranche cleanly.

## What we implemented

### 1. A durable Job executor

DeadReckon now creates a Job before agent work begins. That Job freezes:

- the approved goal and definition of done;
- execution, sandbox and tool policy;
- launch plan;
- source revision and deliverable identity;
- retry, time and spend limits.

Jobs have append-only lifecycle events, fenced leases, heartbeats and explicit stop reasons including cancelled, blocked, budget exhausted, retry exhausted, failed, needs review and lost containment.

The supervisor can reclaim expired leases and recover from several worker, supervisor and launch crash windows. A guarded release handshake prevents repository-controlled commands from running until their process identity has been durably recorded.

Optional launchd/systemd supervisor definitions and management commands also exist, although real reboot recovery is not yet proven.

### 2. One Job model for ordinary execution

The same scheduler now owns:

- single runs;
- orchestration and stored-plan forks;
- newly created chains represented as linear Graph Jobs;
- campaigns.

Graph and Campaign Jobs retain one parent Job ID. Their child work is merged, and the parent result is independently checked, receipted and promoted.

`start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `kill`, `finish` and `report` resolve through shared Job lifecycle truth and suppress duplicate backing runs or plans.

This consolidation is not completely finished: historical chain execution, chain extension, previews, explicit in-place or uncontained work, and some policy-heavy conductor modes remain outside the trusted Job path.

### 3. Two-key completion

A durable Job can only be accepted when both keys agree:

1. The frozen deterministic definition-of-done checks pass inside a real sandbox.
2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge reviews the goal, contract, diff and cited evidence and returns `achieved`.

A failed deterministic check cannot be overruled by the judge. `uncertain`, malformed or unavailable judging produces `NEEDS_REVIEW`.

A Single Job can respond to `revise` with another bounded worker turn. Graph and Campaign parents currently stop for review when the judge says `revise`; automatic parent repair remains unfinished.

The loop also hardened semantic-judge cancellation, time and spend accounting, evidence citation, and structured Codex answers.

### 4. A substantially stronger trust boundary

The completion gate is now split into two phases:

- `dr-gate evaluate` runs without signing material inside the resolved sandbox.
- Only after evaluation and process cleanup does `dr-gate sign` receive the external key.

Implemented protections include:

- HMAC-SHA-256 markers and receipts;
- signing keys outside agent-visible workspaces;
- constant-time signature checking;
- strict refusal when sandbox resolution produces `none`;
- denial of authority, lifecycle, gate, proof, receipt and Git-control paths;
- removal of inherited signing environment variables;
- whole-process-group cancellation and cleanup;
- rejection of synthetic completion markers;
- canonical and symlink path protection;
- fail-closed handling for corrupt or unverifiable process records.

Receipts bind the approved authority, policy, contract, launch plan, source and result revisions, deliverable tree digests, gate evidence, semantic judgment and observed sandbox backend.

### 5. Exact result and promotion identity

The new artifact policy distinguishes:

- deliverable files;
- durable evidence;
- lifecycle metadata;
- disposable runtime/build output.

Trusted copying preserves executable bits, symlinks and raw path identity without following links. It rejects unsupported special files.

Provider-created commits and index state are not trusted as final results. DeadReckon reconstructs its own result commit and checks merge history, filters, gitlinks, dirty indexes, file kind, modes and symlink targets.

Promotion is crash-recoverable and validates the candidate before publication. A rejected worktree delivery can restore the pre-delivery revision.

### 6. Recovery and adversarial coverage

We added tests for:

- two supervisors racing for one Job;
- lease expiry, boot changes and stale epochs;
- every modeled launch and promotion crash window;
- Single, Graph and Campaign identity recovery;
- planner-budget recovery;
- cancellation during semantic judging;
- cancellation and SIGKILL during gate evaluation;
- malformed process records;
- attempted key, proof and control-path tampering;
- forged markers and changed evidence;
- Graph/Campaign parent ownership.

The macOS public-command tests exercise the real Seatbelt path. The credential-free adversarial suite records seven passes and no failures.

The complete workspace verification is still running, but formatting, Clippy, the public API check, the main workspace suites, Watchkeeper ownership/recovery/trust suites, runtime, provider and sandbox tests have passed so far.

## What remains on the docket

### Immediate integration work

The repository currently has:

- 12 Watchkeeper commits on local `main`, ahead of `origin/main`;
- a further uncommitted hardening tranche touching 58 tracked project files plus one new source file;
- approximately 12,300 additions in that uncommitted tranche;
- nothing pushed upstream.

The immediate job is to finish full verification, review the intended diff, commit the hardening tranche without including unrelated user files, and then rerun committed-source adversarial checks. It should not be pushed until that is complete.

### Real dogfooding

This is now the largest missing piece.

The 24-task operator matrix currently records:

- 2 attempted;
- 22 not run;
- 0 verified completions.

We still need real tasks across repositories and providers, measuring:

- unattended verified completion;
- recovery after interruption;
- false acceptance and rejection;
- operator interventions;
- time needed to understand the receipt;
- supervision and judging cost.

### Live failure drills

We still need to prove:

- real launchd/systemd restart and machine reboot recovery;
- Linux/bubblewrap containment;
- Docker containment and cleanup;
- provider/network failure and restoration;
- hostile child-process escape attempts;
- broader cross-provider behavior;
- strict Windows support or an explicit fail-closed refusal.

### Safe Graph and Campaign repair

When the semantic judge says a merged Graph or Campaign result needs revision, the parent currently stops at `NEEDS_REVIEW`.

We need a bounded repair mechanism that preserves the frozen authority, does not silently replan, reruns both completion keys and cannot launder a failed child result.

### Finish the compatibility migration

We must either move these onto Jobs or deliberately label and retain them as untrusted compatibility modes:

- historical `chain run` and `chain resume`;
- chain extension;
- previews;
- explicit in-place and uncontained execution;
- unsupported conductor policies.

They must never accidentally issue a trusted Job receipt.

### Product simplification

Once the kernel is proven:

- keep `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `finish` as the normal surface;
- group advanced operations;
- remove ignored flags, aliases and duplicate lifecycle names;
- consolidate overlapping narration pipelines;
- freeze deeper campaign and learning expansion until usage justifies them.

Rules-as-gate, resource leasing, MCP exposure, handoff artifacts and cross-run analysis are sensible later extensions, but they are not required to prove the central promise.

## Bottom line

We have implemented the machinery behind the intended statement:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

What we have not yet earned is saying that this works reliably in everyday operation. The code and deterministic evidence are substantial; integration, live interruption trials, cross-platform proof and the 24-task dogfood campaign are the remaining credibility boundary.

- Graph and Campaign use the same repair mechanism.

- Multiple consecutive revision rounds are supported and cryptographically chained.
- Repair respects attempt, spend and time limits.
- Cancellation takes precedence over retry.

## Implemented and committed

Fourteen Watchkeeper commits are on the local `main` branch, ending at `6bb8a7d`. They have not been pushed; local `main` is 14 commits ahead of `origin/main`.

### Durable goal execution

DeadReckon now:

- Creates a durable Job with a stable ID.
- Records lifecycle changes in append-only history.
- Leases work to a supervisor and fences stale workers.
- Recovers abandoned work after a process interruption.
- Applies bounded retry, time and spending policies.
- Distinguishes achieved, blocked, cancelled, budget-exhausted and failed.
- Keeps enough state to inspect and continue a job later.

Machine-reboot recovery is designed into the persistence model, but has not yet been demonstrated through a real reboot and installed background service.

### One common job model

The following supported entry points now converge on durable Jobs:

- Direct run → Single Job
- Guided/full-plan execution → Graph Job
- `orchestrate` → Graph Job
- Stored-plan `fork` → Graph Job
- Supported chains → linear Graph Job
- Campaigns → Campaign Job

They share the ordinary operator journey:

```text
start → attach → status/list → finish
```

Older compatibility and preview routes still exist, but trusted unattended execution goes through Jobs.

### Independent completion verification

Completion now has two keys:

1. Compiled deterministic checks must pass.
2. A separate, read-only semantic judge evaluates the goal, contract, changes and evidence.

The semantic judge cannot override failed checks. It can return:

- achieved
- revise
- uncertain / needs review

Graph and Campaign parents can also undergo bounded semantic repair without silently becoming a new Job.

### Gate and receipt protection

The trusted finish boundary now includes:

- HMAC-SHA-256 signing.
- Keys stored outside the agent-visible workspace.
- Receipts bound to the contract, policy and source/result revisions.
- Protected proof and gate paths.
- Fail-closed behavior for trusted unattended execution.
- Lease and attempt lineage checks.
- Rejection of symlink substitution, post-seal mutation, synthetic evidence and stale workers.

### Documentation and operator evidence

- Updated architecture and product-map documentation.
- An operator acceptance checklist.
- Credential-free adversarial tests.
- Characterization coverage for existing chain and orchestration behavior.
- Full workspace tests, formatting, Clippy and release-build verification at the latest committed checkpoint.

## Two local gaps discovered during the audit

These are the immediate engineering docket.

### 1. Job-owned child Runs can bypass their Job

A user can currently address a child Run directly with legacy `resume` or `extend`. That can mutate the child after its parent Job has produced a receipt.

The intended fix is:

- Detect whether the Run belongs to a Job-owned Plan.
- Refuse public mutation outside the active Job driver.
- Direct the operator to `deadreckon attach <job-id>`.
- Preserve legacy behavior for genuinely unowned Runs and Plans.

### 2. Planning is instructed to be read-only but technically receives write access

Plan, chain and campaign decomposition happen before trusted Job execution. Their prompts say not to modify the repository, but some provider requests currently grant `ReadWrite` workspace access.

The intended fix is:

- Give every planning request actual read-only capability.
- Centralize that policy.
- Add hostile-provider tests that deliberately attempt to write.

These are meaningful trust-boundary defects, which is why checkpointing paused while they were traced.

DeadReckon’s core promise is mostly implemented in code. It is not yet fully proven as an operational claim.

The loop produced 14 Watchkeeper commits. They are on `main` through `6bb8a7d`; current Git refs show `origin/main` at the same commit. A final security/lifecycle hardening batch remains uncommitted.

## Implemented and committed

- Durable Jobs with immutable approved authority and append-only event history.
- Detached execution returning a persistent Job ID.
- Lease-fenced supervision, abandoned-lease recovery and bounded retries.
- Explicit terminal states for completed, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted and needs-review.
- Wall-time, attempt, turn and spend enforcement.
- Crash-atomic child launch, including preparation records, release handshakes, PID identity and recovery after supervisor loss.
- One scheduler for:

  - ordinary runs;
  - orchestrations;
  - supported chains;
  - stored-plan forks;
  - campaigns.

- Job-aware `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `kill`, `finish` and reporting.
- Same-ID parent results for Graph and Campaign work.
- Two-key completion:

  1. Contained deterministic checks must pass.
  2. A fresh, independent semantic judge must return `achieved`.

- Semantic results distinguish `achieved`, `revise` and `uncertain`. Missing or malformed judgment becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
- Bounded parent-only repair after a semantic `revise`, without rerunning successful child tasks.
- HMAC-SHA-256 receipts with signing material outside the agent workspace.
- Receipts bind approved authority, policy, checks, source/result identity, semantic judgment, confinement and revisions.
- Promotion and delivery revalidate the receipt rather than trusting the existence of a marker.
- Managed launchd/systemd supervisor definitions and commands.
- Credential-free adversarial dogfood: currently 10 proof groups passing, zero failing and nine live claims explicitly unproven.

The implemented Job model is summarized in [MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:83), with the two-key completion behavior at [line 184](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:184).

## Built now, but not committed yet

The current hardening batch closes two important holes found during the audit:

- Job-owned child Runs now receive durable ownership identity in their first state write. Public commands can no longer bypass the parent Job by directly resuming, extending, finishing, applying, abandoning, cleaning, rewinding or steering a child Run.
- Killing a Job-owned child routes cancellation through the parent Job.
- Planning, definition-of-done drafting, contract inference and repair-planning provider calls now receive an enforced read-only sandbox—not merely a prompt asking them not to write.
- Even Codex and Claude capability probes now run inside that boundary; testing found those probes were previously an unsandboxed write opportunity.
- Hostile tests deliberately attempt workspace modification and confirm it is denied or fails closed.

The ownership record is visible in [state.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/state.rs:97), and the enforceable read-only provider request is in [types.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-providers/src/types.rs:124).

Targeted verification is green:

- Job ownership suite: 11 passed.
- Provider suite: 147 passed.
- Sandbox suite: 25 passed.
- Relevant chain and orchestration regressions passed.

This batch has not yet passed the final whole-workspace gate or been committed.

### Operational proof

The 24-task live dogfood programme is the largest unfinished part. So far it records only 2 attempted tasks, 22 not run and 0 verified completions. We still need to:

- kill a worker during a real provider run;
- kill the supervisor during a real provider run;
- remove host network access mid-call;
- reboot the machine with the service active;
- cause a natural semantic `revise` and observe parent repair;
- interrupt and recover a live Campaign without duplicated work;
- attack the gate through multiple real providers;
- repeat gate containment on Linux/bubblewrap and Docker;
- measure intervention count, comprehension time, recovery rate, judging cost, and false accept/reject rates.

Those boundaries are listed in the [dogfood README](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/examples/watchkeeper-dogfood/README.md:90).

### Product consolidation

Several older modes still sit outside the trusted Job contract:

- preview execution;
- explicit in-place or uncontained execution;
- historical `chain run` and `chain resume`;
- chain extension and policy-rich compatibility behavior.

We need to preserve or intentionally retire those paths. The product surface has converged substantially, but it has not literally collapsed to only `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish`.

## Honest assessment

We have built the necessary machinery: durable state, leases, containment, independent judgment, receipts and recovery invariants.

What remains is no longer primarily “invent the architecture.” It is:

1. finish and commit the current hardening;
2. run destructive live trials;
3. simplify or retire compatibility modes;
4. demonstrate that real users can understand and trust the resulting receipt.

Only after those trials can we honestly make the complete claim:

> Give DeadReckon a goal and an approved definition of done. It will work in isolation, survive interruptions, stop for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear receipt explaining what happened.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 17:10:47Z)**_

The major achievement is architectural: DeadReckon is now a durable control plane around coding agents, rather than merely a CLI that launches and documents them.

We have achieved:

- One approved Job model. The goal, definition of done, budget, provider, isolation policy and delivery target are frozen before work begins.
- Durable detached execution. Jobs have persistent IDs, append-only event histories, fenced leases and recoverable state independent of the launching terminal.
- One scheduler for ordinary runs, orchestrations, supported chains, stored plans and campaigns.
- Bounded autonomy. Attempts, wall time, turns and spend are enforced, with explicit outcomes such as blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted and needs-review.
- Crash-aware recovery. DeadReckon records launch intent, process identity and release acknowledgement so it can recover without casually duplicating work.
- Two-key completion:

  1. Deterministic definition-of-done checks must pass.
  2. An independent semantic judge must confirm that the result actually achieves the approved goal.

- Semantic repair. A `revise` decision can trigger bounded repair— including parent-only Graph/Campaign repair—without rerunning successful leaves.
- Tamper-resistant completion. HMAC-signed receipts bind the approved contract, policy, source, result, checks, semantic judgment, confinement and revisions.
- Protected trust boundaries. Agents cannot access signing keys or write Job/proof authority. The evaluator is keyless; signing happens only after it exits.
- Deliberate delivery. `finish` revalidates the receipt and delivers the receipt-bound result instead of trusting a mutable working directory.
- A coherent operator lifecycle centred on `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish`.
- Child ownership protection. The latest hardening prevents users or agents from bypassing a parent Job by directly mutating one of its child Runs.
- Enforced read-only planning. Planning, contract inference and definition-of-done generation can inspect the repository but cannot modify it—even during provider capability probing.
- Real evidence. The credential-free adversarial matrix now has 11 proof groups passing, zero failing, with nine live claims honestly labelled unproven.

In practical terms, the supported path is now close to this:

> Approve a goal and definition of done, receive a Job ID, close the terminal, return later, and inspect a bounded, independently verified result with a signed explanation of what happened.

What we have not yet earned is the unrestricted real-world claim. Machine reboot recovery, live provider interruption, Linux/Docker containment, cross-provider attacks and the full 24-task dogfood programme still require operator trials.

## What we have achieved

| Area | Current achievement |
|---|---|
| Durable execution | Supported work now runs as durable Jobs with append-only history, fenced leases, recovery logic, bounded retries, time/spend limits and explicit terminal reasons. |
| Independent completion | A Job must pass deterministic checks and then receive an independent semantic judgment. A failed check cannot be overruled by the LLM judge. |
| Secure verification | Gate keys live outside the workspace. Receipts use HMAC-SHA-256 and bind the contract, policy, sandbox, revisions, result tree and evidence. Synthetic or tampered proof is rejected. |
| Unified job model | Direct runs, orchestration, stored-plan forks, supported chains and campaigns now use the same Job scheduler and parent verification model. |
| Operator experience | Jobs can be found and controlled through the shared `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `kill` and `finish` lifecycle. `JobView` and `RunView` reconstruct what happened from durable evidence. |
| Isolation and delivery | Workers operate in isolated workspaces and sandboxes. Strict verified Jobs refuse an uncontained `none` sandbox. Promotion into the target repository is deliberate and revalidated. |
| Recovery of complex work | Single, Graph and Campaign Jobs can recover persisted state. Graph and Campaign parents support bounded semantic revision without rerunning already successful leaves. |
| Evidence and receipts | Runs retain events, spend, traces, snapshots, diffs, judgments, stop reasons and final receipts rather than leaving only terminal output. |
| Adversarial testing | The committed credential-free suite records 11 passes, 0 failures and 9 explicitly unproven live claims. The last clean checkpoint passed approximately 2,443 tests and the release-size gate. |

A particularly important achievement is that DeadReckon no longer treats “the coding CLI exited successfully” as completion. Completion is now owned by DeadReckon and requires:

```text
approved goal and contract
        ↓
isolated durable Job
        ↓
contained deterministic checks
        ↓
independent semantic assessment
        ↓
signed receipt
        ↓
deliberate promotion
```

## What we have achieved

- An approved goal and definition of done are frozen before work begins.
- Supported work launches as a durable Job, returns one Job ID, and detaches.

Completion now has two keys:

1. Contained deterministic checks must pass.
2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge must find that the result actually satisfies the goal.

Deterministic failure cannot be overruled. The semantic judge can return `achieved`, `revise` or `uncertain`; uncertainty and judge failure stop as `NEEDS_REVIEW`. Graph and Campaign parents can undergo bounded parent-only repair without rerunning successful children.

The trust boundary is substantially stronger:

- HMAC-SHA-256 signing keys live outside the agent workspace.
- Receipts bind the approved contract, policy, source/result identity, result-tree digest, semantic judgment and actual sandbox backend.

- Forged markers, symlink substitution, result mutation and uncontained strict runs fail closed.

- sandbox wrappers could be impersonated through `PATH`;
- macOS evaluation could write outside the workspace;
- verdict evaluation inherited ambient secrets;
- Docker lacked necessary gate/runtime mounts;
- bubblewrap attempted nonexistent macOS paths on Linux.

Focused macOS, verdict, Docker and sandbox tests pass after those changes.

The last full baseline passed 2,443 tests before the newest containment changes. Since then, focused verification includes:

## What is not yet achieved

The biggest gap is operational proof.

We have not yet demonstrated all of this through:

- a real machine reboot with service-backed recovery;
- live Linux/bubblewrap execution;
- a public strict Docker Job;
- real cross-provider gate attacks;
- network removal during active work;

- measured false-accept and false-reject rates.

The new live-trial recorder is useful scaffolding, but its audit found a blocker: a “passed” result currently proves consistency among operator-supplied files, not that the fault, reboot or process interruption actually happened. Those files can be manufactured without a live process. It also does not yet enforce backend/provider/replay identity strongly enough, and 5 of its 9 claims are deliberately incapable of passing.

## Necessary versus incidental complexity

Necessary complexity is now mostly in the right places:

- durable event histories;
- leases and process identity;
- isolation;
- bounded policies;
- deterministic plus semantic verification;
- tamper-resistant receipts.

The remaining incidental complexity is:

- legacy run/chain paths alongside the Job model;
- too many advanced top-level surfaces;
- overlapping narration and learning features;
- documentation drifting from executable behaviour;
- a large standalone recorder compensating for missing trusted event producers.

The recorder should be simplified around a trusted, append-only capture envelope emitted by DeadReckon itself—not expanded with more checks over mutable operator files.

The core mechanism is largely built. For supported durable Job paths, DeadReckon can already freeze authority, work in isolation, enforce bounds, verify checks and meaning, and produce a signed receipt.

What we cannot honestly say yet is that the entire promise survives real machine/provider/backend failures in ordinary use. The short answer: we have built most of DeadReckon’s durable execution system, but we have not yet proved the complete product promise in real-world operation.

## What we have achieved

- A goal becomes a durable Job before coding begins. Its approved goal, definition of done, limits, source, sandbox policy, and execution shape are frozen.
- Jobs detach and continue under a local supervisor with leases, bounded attempts, time limits, and spending limits.
- Single runs, ordinary graphs, new chains, stored-plan forks, and campaigns largely use the same Job scheduler.
- Completion requires two independent keys:
  1. deterministic checks pass inside containment;
  2. a fresh, read-only semantic judge says the result actually satisfies the goal.
- Deterministic failure cannot be overruled by the LLM judge.
- Results receive an HMAC-authenticated receipt binding the contract, source and result trees, sandbox, checks, judgment, policy, and revision.
- `finish` revalidates that receipt and the delivery history before promoting work.
- Worker and supervisor crash windows have been substantially closed using process identity, boot identity, launch tokens, fenced leases, and append-only events.
- Graph and Campaign parents can perform bounded semantic repair without rerunning successful children.
- Explicit outcomes distinguish verified, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted, lost containment, and needs-review conditions.
- Per-user launchd/systemd supervisor management exists.
- `supervisor status --json` now provides typed reboot evidence and rejects forged, malformed, symlinked, test-overridden, or mismatched service state.
- Hostile path, receipt-forgery, process-cleanup, macOS Seatbelt, and Docker-boundary tests have been added.

The central achievement is that “the coding agent says it is done” is no longer DeadReckon’s definition of completion. DeadReckon owns the lifecycle and acceptance decision independently. That architecture is described in the [current map](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:83) and [Watchkeeper changelog](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/CHANGELOG.md:55).

## Necessary versus incidental complexity

The necessary complexity is:

- immutable authority;
- append-only lifecycle truth;
- leases and process identity;
- containment;
- bounded policies;
- deterministic plus semantic verification;
- signed receipts;
- crash-safe recovery.

Without those, the high-level promise is not trustworthy.

The incidental complexity has been:

- retaining numerous historical execution paths;
- exposing too many orchestration concepts as peer CLI commands;
- Campaign depth before the basic live promise was fully proven;

## What we have achieved

- A durable Job model now owns execution. Jobs have stable IDs, append-only histories, leases, retries, budgets, process supervision and explicit terminal reasons such as blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted and needs-review.
- Jobs can detach from the launching shell. A per-user supervisor can install, start, stop, inspect and resume queued work.
- Ordinary runs, orchestrations, new chains, stored-plan forks and campaigns mostly pass through the same Job scheduler.
- Completion now has two keys:
  1. The compiled deterministic definition-of-done checks must pass.
  2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge must conclude that the result actually achieves the goal.
- The semantic judge cannot override failed checks. Uncertain, malformed or unavailable judgment becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
- Completion produces an HMAC-signed receipt binding the goal, contract, policy, source revision, result revision, deliverable tree, deterministic evidence, semantic judgment and actual sandbox backend.
- `finish` validates that receipt before applying or exporting work. Mutated, synthetic, stale or mismatched evidence fails closed.
- Strict Jobs run in isolated workspaces with protected signing, authority, proof and lifecycle paths. We have a real macOS Seatbelt test proving containment, environment scrubbing and process cleanup.
- Graph and Campaign Jobs now have parent-level verification rather than treating successful children as proof that the combined result is correct.
- Advanced work has bounded parent repair: semantic `revise` can repair the merged result without rerunning successful children.
- Campaign launch, adoption, lease fencing, cancellation and crash-window recovery have been substantially hardened.
- The operator surface is converging on `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish`, with detailed state, evidence and receipts underneath.

There are 15 Watchkeeper commits already pushed to `main` and `origin/main`. The current hardening wave is in the shared working tree and is not yet committed.

## What the current hardening wave adds

Implemented and compiling, but still under final review:

- authenticated operator capture for destructive reboot, network and process-kill trials;
- deterministic replay of captured evidence before a trial may be marked successful;
- sandbox observations bound directly into completion receipts;
- stronger supervisor/service restart evidence;
- crash-safe Campaign child adoption;
- owned and contained Graph/Campaign repair workers;
- denial of agent access to operator-capture evidence;
- additional lineage, publication and tamper checks.

These changes are significant, but they should not yet be described as integrated or complete until the overlapping edits pass the combined suite and are committed in scoped changes.

## What has actually been proved

The committed credential-free adversarial suite currently records:

- 11 passed claims;
- 0 failed claims;
- 9 live or host-dependent claims still unproven.

The live trial matrix currently records:

- 2 attempted tasks;
- 22 not run;
- 0 verified end-to-end results.

We have strong hermetic and focused test evidence, plus a real macOS sandbox trial. We do not yet have adequate evidence for:

- a real machine reboot and service recovery;
- Linux/bubblewrap execution;
- a public strict Docker Job;

- multiple real providers and repositories;
- false-acceptance and false-rejection rates;
- the planned 20–30 unattended dogfood tasks.

## The honest product assessment

We can now credibly say:

> DeadReckon can turn an approved goal into a durable isolated Job, require deterministic and semantic verification, stop for typed reasons, and produce a tamper-resistant completion receipt.

We cannot yet responsibly claim the complete target statement:

> It will reliably survive arbitrary interruptions and run unattended to verified completion across supported machines and providers.

That last gap is now mostly proof, integration and compatibility retirement—not missing architecture.

The essential complexity is the durable Job kernel, leases, isolation, two-key verification and signed receipts. The incidental complexity is concentrated in legacy execution paths, separate Graph/Campaign recovery logic, the very broad CLI and older narration/learning surfaces. Once this hardening wave is integrated, the highest-value next step is to freeze feature expansion, retire or quarantine the remaining legacy mutation routes, and run the real dogfood matrix.

We have successfully built most of the core system promised by this goal. We have not yet completed the live, real-world proof that lets us call the entire goal finished.

### What is working

| Original objective | Achievement |
|---|---|
| Durable goal executor | Jobs are saved before work begins, receive an ID, detach, use fenced ownership, reclaim abandoned work, enforce bounded attempts/time/spend, and record explicit terminal reasons. |
| Semantic second key | Deterministic checks must pass first. A separate read-only semantic judge must then return `achieved`; `revise`, `uncertain`, unavailable, and malformed results cannot silently pass. |
| Tamper-resistant gate | Gate secrets are kept outside the working area. Markers and receipts use HMAC-SHA-256 and bind the contract, policy, revisions, semantic judgment, containment backend, and exact result tree. |
| One Job model | Ordinary runs, guided review/full-plan work, direct orchestration, stored-plan forks, supported chains, and campaigns now enter the same durable scheduler. |
| Recovery | We implemented lease expiry/reclaim, process identity checks, crash-atomic child launch, candidate recovery, and bounded Graph/Campaign parent repair. |
| Operator surface | `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `finish`, and supervisor service commands exist. `finish` refuses delivery without a valid receipt. |
| Evidence | Jobs leave append-only history, state projections, deterministic evidence, semantic judgments, receipts, logs, and operator-facing documentation. |

We have successfully built most of the intended DeadReckon execution model. The remaining work is mainly integration, evidence refresh, and real-world fault testing—not inventing the core architecture.

What is working:

- One durable Job model now underpins guided `start`, ordinary `run`, orchestration, stored-plan forks, supported chains, and campaigns.
- Jobs are persisted before work starts, receive one stable ID, detach to a supervisor, and can be inspected through `attach`, `status`, `list`, `report`, and `finish`.
- The supervisor uses fenced leases, renews them, reclaims abandoned work, avoids duplicate child launches, and preserves explicit retry, wall-time, spend, cancellation, failure, and review outcomes.
- Completion requires both deterministic checks and an independent read-only semantic judge. Failed checks cannot be overruled; uncertainty or judge failure becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
- HMAC-SHA-256 receipts bind the approved contract, policy, source and result identity, gate evidence, semantic judgment, and actual sandbox backend.
- Signing material and Job control paths are kept outside the worker’s writable workspace.
- Promotion and `finish` validate the receipt and exact result identity before delivering anything.
- Graph and Campaign results are verified at the parent level. Campaign roll-ups are reconstructed and checked, and semantic repair has bounded, recoverable, tamper-checked lineage.
- Launchd and systemd supervisor-service support exists, although actual reboot recovery remains a live-test claim.
- A dogfood framework now exists with 24 tasks, an adversarial runner, operator acceptance instructions, and a passive fault-trial recorder.

- `extend` now queues a durable child Job and binds it to the parent’s verified receipt and promoted source tree.
- Parent-state, receipt, or source-tree tampering stops an extension before child evidence is created.
- Public legacy `resume`, `merge`, and Campaign repair routes refuse unowned mutation before touching artifacts.
- `orchestrate --preview` is now genuinely read-only and does not create plans, Jobs, accounting records, or workspaces.

We have successfully built most of the core machinery. We have not yet proven the complete product promise under real providers, machine restarts and a representative dogfood run.

### Successfully implemented

- A durable `Job` model with append-only lifecycle events, leases, retry fencing and state reconstruction.
- Detached-by-default execution for the ordinary `start → list/status → attach → finish` journey.
- Explicit terminal outcomes including achieved, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget exhausted and needs review.
- Recovery from killed workers and replacement supervisors in controlled tests.
- Bounded retry, time and spend policies.
- Runs, plans, chains, campaigns and follow-ups routed through Jobs for the supported modern paths.
- Deterministic definition-of-done checks followed by an independent, read-only semantic judge.
- Semantic results of `achieved`, `revise` and `uncertain`; judge failure becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`, not success.
- Bounded semantic repair attempts tied to the original parent Job.
- HMAC-SHA-256 completion receipts binding the goal, contract, policy, authority, source revision, result revision, checks, semantic judgment and sandbox observation.
- Signing material stored outside the agent workspace, with active tests attempting to discover or forge it.
- Sandbox restrictions covering gate keys, receipts, control state and operator evidence.
- Tampered receipts and repair lineage are rejected.
- A protected operator-capture mechanism and a written acceptance procedure.

### What the evidence proves

The credential-free adversarial suite currently records:

- 12 proof groups passed
- 0 failed
- 9 explicitly unproven

Those passing groups include terminal detachment, worker termination, supervisor replacement, network denial, gate-key attacks, Docker control-boundary checks, receipt mutation, result delivery, unified Job routing and semantic parent repair.

The complete committed workspace test suite passed. The live macOS trust-boundary suite also passed 6/6.

The main implementation tranche is committed locally as `9b786d8`—88 files and roughly 26,500 additions. Local `main` is one commit ahead of `origin/main`; it has not been pushed. There is also one small uncommitted fix preserving the true approval provenance of guided continuations, with its targeted test passing.

### What we have not successfully demonstrated yet

- Actual restart through installed launchd/systemd supervision and a machine reboot.
- Live provider recovery after worker termination, network failure and supervisor restart.
- Cross-provider hostile-agent testing.
- Linux/bubblewrap parity and a complete strict public Docker Job.
- A representative 20–30-task dogfood run.

The 24-task dogfood matrix exists, but only two tasks have been attempted, neither reached verified completion, and 22 remain unrun. Consequently, we do not yet have trustworthy completion-rate, recovery-rate, false-acceptance, intervention or cost metrics.

There is also a scope caveat: the supported modern paths converge on Jobs, but some historical, preview and explicitly foreground/uncontained paths remain process-owned.

So the honest assessment is: **the durable execution and verification architecture is substantially built and heavily tested; operational proof of the full promise remains unfinished.** The exact operator trials are documented in [WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md).

Short answer: we have built most of the promised DeadReckon control plane. The core architecture works and is heavily tested. The goal remains active because cross-platform Docker execution and real-world operator trials are not finished.

| Original promise | Current achievement |
|---|---|
| Start work durably and detach | Implemented |
| Run in an isolated workspace | Implemented |
| Recover after worker/supervisor interruption | Implemented and fault-tested |
| Stop for bounded, explicit reasons | Implemented |
| Enforce deterministic definition-of-done checks | Implemented |
| Independently judge whether the result means the goal was achieved | Implemented |
| Produce a tamper-resistant receipt | Implemented |
| Use one model for runs, plans, chains and campaigns | Mostly implemented |
| Survive real reboot/provider/network failures | Designed, but live trials remain |
| Work through strict Docker on every supported host | Not yet; one concrete blocker remains |

### What we successfully built

- A durable Job model with immutable authority, append-only events, fenced leases, bounded retries, budgets and explicit terminal reasons such as blocked, cancelled, failed and budget-exhausted.
- Detached execution: closing the launching terminal does not stop the Job.
- Recovery of abandoned leases, interrupted child launches and persisted Graph/Campaign plans.
- One supervisory model for ordinary runs, orchestration, new chains, plan forks and campaigns.
- A consistent operator surface around `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `kill` and `finish`.
- Refusal of legacy chain operations that could bypass the trusted Job path. These now stop before altering state, Git or the workspace and offer a durable replacement schedule.
- Two-key completion:
  1. Contained deterministic checks must pass.
  2. A fresh, read-only semantic judge must return `achieved`.
- Deterministic failures cannot be overruled by the semantic judge. `revise` can initiate bounded repair; unavailable or uncertain judging becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`.
- HMAC-SHA-256 markers and receipts binding the approved contract, policy, source revision, result revision, result-tree digest, sandbox result and semantic judgment.
- Protection of signing keys, Job authority, proofs and receipt paths from the delegated agent.
- Crash-atomic process and child ownership, including cancellation and retry of nested gate evaluators.
- Explicit promotion: verified work is not delivered until its receipt and authority have been revalidated.
- Protected operator-capture tooling and an adversarial dogfood suite.
- Documentation reconciled around the as-built Job architecture, including the [current project map](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:86) and [operator acceptance procedure](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md:188).

### What has been proven

- The complete Rust workspace test suite passes.
- The main CLI suite passes all 870 tests.
- The live-trial collector passes all 29 tests.
- The clean-source credential-free adversarial run records:
  - 12 passed
  - 0 failed
  - 9 explicitly unproven
- That evidence was generated from a clean detached source revision and committed separately, preventing the evidence from “proving itself.”
- The goal run has produced 19 commits touching 165 files. All are on local `main`; the first 16 are already on `origin/main`, while the latest three remain local and unpushed.

### What is not yet successful

The most immediate blocker is strict Docker completion on macOS. DeadReckon currently passes the host’s macOS `dr-gate` executable into a Linux container. Linux correctly refuses that Mach-O binary. We have localized the problem precisely; it is not an unexplained failure.

The trustworthy fix needs to:

- package Linux ARM64 and x86-64 evaluator binaries;
- select the evaluator matching the Docker image platform;
- bind its digest and platform into the Job authority and receipt;
- run Docker from an immutable cached image with no pulling;
- preserve cancellation and cleanup of daemon-owned containers;
- package and sign all helper binaries correctly across release channels.

The real operator matrix also remains incomplete: 22 of 24 live tasks have not been run, and the two attempted live-provider tasks did not reach a receipt. Outstanding trials include supervisor death, worker death, network loss, reboot recovery, cross-provider gate attacks, live semantic repair, Campaign recovery, Linux bubblewrap and the public strict-Docker journey.

So the honest assessment is: **the durable execution and verification system has been built; operational portability and real-world acceptance are the remaining work.** We should not yet claim the full product promise as achieved.

### Successfully implemented and committed locally

- One durable Job model for ordinary runs, orchestrations, stored-plan forks, supported chains, campaigns and follow-up runs.
- Immutable Job authority plus an append-only event history as lifecycle truth.
- Fenced leases, abandoned-lease recovery and protection against two supervisors owning the same Job.
- Detached execution that survives the launching terminal closing.
- Typed terminal outcomes: verified, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget exhausted, retry exhausted and needs review.
- Enforced attempt, time and spend limits.
- Isolation through worktrees and supported sandbox backends.
- Two-key completion:
  1. deterministic checks must pass;
  2. a fresh, read-only semantic judge must say the goal was achieved.
- HMAC-authenticated completion receipts bound to the Job, contract, policy, source revision, result and semantic judgment.
- Fail-closed promotion: `finish` revalidates the receipt and result before exporting work.
- Normal operator controls through `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, cancellation and `finish`.
- Durable parent verification and bounded semantic repair for Graph and Campaign Jobs.
- Supervisor service install/start/status/stop commands for launchd and systemd.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 17:10:47Z)**_

The practical difference is that DeadReckon will become a durable operator, not just a wrapper around a coding CLI.

You will be able to give it a goal plus an approved definition of done, receive a Job ID immediately, close the terminal, and expect the work to continue in an isolated workspace. If the worker or supervisor dies, it can recover from recorded history instead of forgetting where it was.

More specifically, it will be able to:

- Run ordinary tasks, plans, and chains through the same durable Job lifecycle.
- Prevent two supervisors from executing the same work simultaneously.
- Stop for named reasons such as blocked, cancelled, out of budget, out of time, failed, or needs review.
- Require both deterministic checks and an independent read-only semantic judgment before calling work complete.
- Keep the agent away from the policy, signing key, gate evidence, and receipt it would otherwise be able to tamper with.
- Leave a signed receipt binding the approved goal, checks, source revision, result revision, policy, judge decision, and delivery.
- Preserve ordered chain behavior inside an isolated candidate repository, without incrementally modifying your checkout.
- Freeze chain hooks before launch, run each approved hook once, and block rather than replay it when a crash leaves its external effect uncertain.
- Undo the exact revision delivered by a verified Job, rather than trusting mutable or ambiguous run state.
- Let you understand the outcome through `status`, `attach`, and `finish` without reconstructing it from logs.

Before this work, pieces of that existed, but they were split across runs, plans, campaigns, chains, mutable projections, and process-local conductors. The important new capability is the combined guarantee: **detached execution + crash recovery + isolation + bounded stopping + independent verification + a trustworthy receipt**.

Most of that foundation is now implemented. I am currently wiring the last chain-hook execution/recovery seam, while the parallel lane implements verified Job-ID undo; neither is being counted as finished until the integrated tests prove it.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 17:10:47Z)**_

The big change is this:

> DeadReckon is becoming a durable local execution system, rather than a CLI wrapper that must remain alive while another coding agent works.

| Before | After these enhancements |
|---|---|
| Execution was closely tied to the active terminal/process. | `start` creates a Job, returns its ID and detaches. |
| An interruption could strand the work. | A supervisor can reclaim abandoned work and continue it without running it twice. |
| Runs, Plans and Chains had different lifecycle machinery. | They use the same Job, scheduler, history and receipt model. |
| Passing compiled checks could be treated as completion. | Completion requires both deterministic checks and an independent semantic judge. |
| An unavailable judge could leave an ambiguous result. | It becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`, never silently accepted. |
| Work could reach the repository through several paths. | Work stays in an isolated candidate workspace until verification permits delivery. |
| Evidence documented what happened but had weaker trust boundaries. | A signed receipt binds the goal, definition of done, policy, source revision, result revision, checks, judgment and delivery. |
| Hooks could create uncertain side effects after a crash. | Hook definitions are frozen, invocations recorded, and uncertain outcomes block recovery safely. |
| Undo was tied to older run/chain concepts. | `deadreckon undo <job-id>` reverts exactly the revision proven by that Job’s receipt. |
| Failure was often a generic execution failure. | Jobs stop for explicit reasons such as blocked, cancelled, failed, budget exhausted or needs review. |

A practical future interaction looks like:

```text
deadreckon start goal.md
Created job job_1234

# The terminal may close.

deadreckon status job_1234
deadreckon attach job_1234
deadreckon finish job_1234
```

DeadReckon will retain the history needed to answer:

- What did the agent try?
- What changed?
- Which checks passed?
- Did the result actually satisfy the stated goal?
- Why did execution stop?
- Was anything delivered to the real repository?
- Can that exact delivery be safely undone?

The most important new ability is not merely “keep an agent running.” It is:

> Keep an agent working independently while preserving enough authority, evidence and recovery state that DeadReckon can decide whether the result is safe to accept.

The honest current status is that most of the durable Job, isolation, verification, receipt and recovery foundation has landed. The current worktree also contains the new durable Chain-hook integration and Job-ID undo; it compiles, but still needs focused tests, full repository verification and a commit. Real reboot acceptance, additional judge/gate crash tests, signing-key lifecycle hardening and final adversarial dogfooding remain before we can claim the entire promise is proven end to end.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 17:18:37Z)**_

The Job undo path should not ship yet. It improves substantially on Chain undo, but has three release-blocking authority/idempotency defects.

Reference sibling: `chain_undo_command` confirms, writes a started event, reverts, then projects the object as `Undone` at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/chain/mod.rs:3421-3518`. The intended Job difference is that authority comes from verified receipt-bound delivery evidence. The new code matches confirmation and event recording, but the authority and projected after-state are incomplete.

## P0 — release blockers

1. Apply can succeed without durable undo authority, and merely repeating `finish` can poison a valid ledger.

Git is mutated before `ResultApplied` is recorded at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/lifecycle.rs:1831-1861`. A crash, failed receipt revalidation, or autostash-restore error after the commit leaves no delivery fact.

On retry, `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/lifecycle.rs:1715-1731` treats an empty diff—or any diff command error because of `unwrap_or_default()`—as “already applied” and records `destination_revision_before == resulting_revision`. The same thing happens when an operator simply runs `finish` twice. This creates a second, no-op `ResultApplied` event.

Undo then either refuses multiple deliveries at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:205-218` or refuses the no-op authority at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:238-242`. Exact recovery has been permanently lost even though the first delivery was valid.

Smallest fix: persist a prepared applied-delivery transaction before touching Git. It must bind Job, receipt, destination, target ref, original HEAD and strategy. Reconcile that transaction after interruption and append exactly one final delivery fact. A repeated `finish` must verify and reuse the existing fact, never manufacture a second before/after pair.

2. The claimed “receipt-bound applied revision” is not authenticated.

The signed completion receipt authenticates the candidate source/result revisions. The operator destination, pre-delivery SHA and actual applied SHA exist only in ordinary JSONL detail at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/job.rs:420-430`.

Undo checks that this unsigned event contains the current receipt digest and copies of three signed fields at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:220-237`. Hashing a signed receipt into an unsigned event does not authenticate the event. Someone able to alter Job history can replace destination/before/applied SHAs while retaining the valid receipt fields. Undo also does not re-prove that the substituted applied commit contains only the signed candidate delta.

Smallest fix: create an HMAC-authenticated applied-delivery receipt after delivery. Bind:

- Job and run ID
- completion-receipt SHA
- canonical repository identity and target ref
- pre-delivery and resulting SHAs
- candidate source/result revisions and policy
- delivery strategy

Undo should verify this new receipt and independently revalidate the delivered delta before mutation.

3. Undo does not bind the delivered branch/ref and can revert the wrong ref.

`AppliedDeliveryAuthority` has no branch or symbolic-ref identity at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:12-21`, even though apply knows the target at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/lifecycle.rs:1708-1709`.

Undo checks only repository path, cleanliness and `HEAD` at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:328-342` and `:380-411`. If the operator switches to another branch pointing at the same applied SHA—or detaches HEAD there—undo creates a valid revert on that other ref. The originally delivered branch remains unchanged while DeadReckon records success.

Smallest fix: record and authenticate the full target ref during delivery. Require the same attached ref during undo; reject detached or alternate branches even when their SHA matches.

## P1 — serious safety and lifecycle gaps

4. Job projection continues to report “applied” after successful undo.

The reducer deliberately ignores all undo events at `crates/deadreckon-core/src/job.rs:583-590`. Status therefore still renders the delivery as applied at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/job.rs:608-657`, and `job_primary_action` continues treating any delivery as complete at `:671-684`.

This differs from the working Chain sibling, which records `ChainStatus::Undone` at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/chain/mod.rs:3491-3502`. It also leaves `finish` free to reapply or append another delivery.

Add a typed projected undo state containing status, operation ID, applied SHA, undo SHA, time and failure reason. `UndoCompleted` should mark the delivery undone. A later re-delivery should require an explicit redo/reapply transition, not ordinary `finish`.

5. The operation lock does not serialize delivery against undo, and Git mutation has a TOCTOU window.

Undo’s lock at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:67-94` is private to this authority. Apply/finish does not acquire it. A second delivery can be appended after authority validation, and finish or an external Git process can change `HEAD` between the check at `:328-342` and `git revert` at `:357-369`.

If that happens, Git may successfully create a revert atop another commit. The after-check at `:370-375` detects the mismatch only after the repository has already been mutated.

The generic lock also unlocks before removing its path at `crates/deadreckon-core/src/lock.rs:59-65`, allowing an old-inode/new-inode race between successive acquirers.

Use one shared destination transaction lock for apply, finish and undo. More importantly, construct the revert against the expected SHA and update the authenticated target ref with a compare-and-swap (`old == applied SHA`), so a concurrent ref change prevents mutation.

6. “Clean” is not strong enough, and mutable Git configuration can affect the result.

`require_clean_exact_destination` relies only on porcelain status at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:401-409`. It does not prove the absence of:

- changes hidden by `assume-unchanged` or `skip-worktree`;
- an in-progress merge/cherry-pick/revert;
- a substituted Git index/environment;
- hook or fsmonitor side effects.

There is no final cleanliness check after `git revert` at `:369-377`, so a post-commit hook can leave operator dirt while undo records success.

There is also a concrete signing-hardening bug: undo prefixes its arguments with `-c revert.reference=false` at `:357-369`. `hardened_git_prefix` finds the first non-dash argument at `crates/deadreckon-core/src/git.rs:50-62`, mistakes `revert.reference=false` for the verb and therefore does not add `commit.gpgsign=false`. A configured signer can run or fail after partial mutation.

Sanitize Git control environment, disable mutable hooks/signing/fsmonitor for this operation, detect hidden index flags and in-progress operations, and verify clean exact state again before recording completion. A plumbing-based revert commit plus atomic ref update would be safer than porcelain `git revert`.

## P2 — evidence and interface integrity

7. Malformed undo histories are not rejected as invalid transitions.

`undo_history_state` at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:259-325`:

- accepts `UndoCompleted` or `UndoFailed` without a preceding start;
- accepts both failed and completed terminal events for one operation;
- compares only authority digest and operation ID, not the complete typed authority;
- silently ignores undo events carrying another authority digest.

The core reducer ignores these events entirely. Move transition validation into the append/reducer boundary with typed, versioned detail and fail closed on impossible ordering.

8. Crash recovery can claim an operator-created revert as DeadReckon’s own.

`is_exact_revert_commit` checks only parent, tree and the default Git message at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:414-438`. It does not bind the revert commit to the durable operation ID. A manually created exact revert is adopted and recorded as a recovered DeadReckon operation.

Include Job ID, operation ID and authority digest in a deterministic commit trailer, and require that trailer during recovery.

9. Public argument routing needs one destructive-command safeguard.

The shared reference resolver correctly resolves Jobs before their same-ID backing Runs. However, `crates/deadreckon/src/main.rs:1479-1485` silently uses the positional ID when both positional ID and deprecated `--run` are supplied. For a destructive command, conflicting identifiers should be rejected by clap.

## Missing tests

Existing tests at `crates/deadreckon/src/commands/undo.rs:681-845` cover basic idempotence, the post-commit/pre-completion crash window, legacy unbound evidence, one untracked dirty file and an in-memory policy mismatch. The fixture uses a fake signature and calls the private helper, so it does not prove the public HMAC-validated path.

Required tests before acceptance:

- genuine sealed receipt → real `finish` → public `undo <job-id>`;
- crash after Git apply but before `ResultApplied`, followed by finish and undo recovery;
- repeat `finish` before undo: exactly one delivery fact;
- autostash restoration failure after apply;
- second branch and detached HEAD at the same applied SHA;
- undo racing finish, another undo and an external HEAD update;
- staged, unstaged, untracked, assume-unchanged and skip-worktree dirt;
- merge/revert/cherry-pick in-progress state;
- moved repository, symlink substitution and same-path replacement;
- commit-signing, commit-msg, post-commit and fsmonitor interference;
- tampered destination/before/applied delivery fields with an otherwise valid completion receipt;
